summary: This script defines two utility functions for validation: one checks that a variable isn't empty and prints an error message if it is, and the other verifies that a command-line tool (binary) exists on the system, exiting with an error if it doesn't. These are helper functions you'd call at the start of a script to ensure prerequisites are met.

explanations.4: The ${1:-} syntax means 'use the first argument, but if it's not provided, use an empty string instead'. The -r flag makes the variable read-only so it can't be accidentally modified.
explanations.5: This captures an optional second argument as the error message, but if none is provided, it defaults to a generic message about empty variables.
explanations.7: [[ -z ${variable} ]] tests whether the variable is empty (zero length). The && operator means 'if the test is true, then execute the echo command'. The >&2 redirects the output to stderr (error stream) instead of stdout.
explanations.13: Same pattern as line 4—capture the first argument and make it read-only, defaulting to empty string if not provided.
explanations.15: This calls the assert::notEmpty function we defined earlier, passing the binary name and a custom error message, using backslash to continue the command onto the next line.
explanations.18: command -v returns the path to a binary if it exists, or nothing if it doesn't. The || true ensures the command doesn't fail if the binary isn't found (which would normally cause the script to exit). The [[ -z ... ]] checks if the result is empty.
explanations.20: exit 1 stops the entire script and signals that an error occurred (non-zero exit code).
